Richter's Predictor: Modeling Earthquake Damage¶

Predicting Earthquake Building Damage Grades¶

Problem Statement¶

On 25 April 2015, a magnitude-7.8 earthquake struck Nepal. In its aftermath, Kathmandu Living Labs and the Central Bureau of Statistics (under Nepal's National Planning Commission) surveyed hundreds of thousands of buildings to record the damage each one sustained. Manually assessing every building at this scale is far too slow, so the goal of this project is to predict a building's damage grade automatically from its structural, geographic, and ownership characteristics.

The target, damage_grade, is an ordinal variable with three levels:

Grade Meaning
1 Low damage
2 Medium damage
3 Near-total destruction

This is a multi-class (ordinal) classification problem built on one of the largest post-disaster survey datasets ever collected. It mixes heavily categorical structural features (foundation type, roof material, land surface condition, legal ownership) with hierarchical geo-location IDs and normalized numeric features, more real-world messiness than a typical tabular-ML dataset.

Dataset at a glance

Rows Columns
train_values + train_labels 260,601 39
test_values 86,868 39
Combined 347,469 75% / 25% train-test split

Feature Description¶

Each building is described by 38 features (plus the building_id identifier), grouped as follows:

Group Count Examples
Geographic (hierarchical) 3 geo_level_1_id (0-30) -> geo_level_2_id (0-1427) -> geo_level_3_id (0-12567)
Numeric building characteristics 5 count_floors_pre_eq, age, area_percentage, height_percentage, count_families
Categorical building characteristics 8 land_surface_condition, foundation_type, roof_type, ground_floor_type, other_floor_type, position, plan_configuration, legal_ownership_status
Superstructure material flags (binary) 11 has_superstructure_mud_mortar_stone, has_superstructure_timber, has_superstructure_rc_engineered, ...
Secondary-use flags (binary) 11 has_secondary_use (umbrella) plus 10 sub-flags: _agriculture, _hotel, _rental, _institution, _school, _industry, _health_post, _gov_office, _use_police, _other

The geo-location IDs form a strict three-level hierarchy (every geo_level_3_id nests inside exactly one geo_level_2_id, which nests inside exactly one geo_level_1_id), which is why they're target/frequency encoded rather than one-hot encoded. The 8 categorical columns are all low-cardinality (3-10 levels) and are one-hot encoded instead.

Project Roadmap¶

A. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

  1. Load the training features, training labels, and test features.
  2. Confirm ID integrity: unique identifiers within each set, no overlap between train and test, and row-alignment between features and labels.
  3. Inspect shape, columns, and dtypes.
  4. Check missing values.
  5. Check duplicate rows (full duplicates and feature-level duplicates).
  6. Check invalid / sentinel values.
  7. Analyse distributions of individual features.
  8. Analyse the target variable: class balance / shape, and its implications for metric choice and cross-validation strategy.
  9. Check cardinality and structure of any hierarchical or high-cardinality features -- this will decide encoding strategy later.
  10. Check relationships / correlations between features and the target.
  11. Summarise data-quality findings and their modeling implications.

B. Cleaning¶

  1. Define deterministic cleaning rules from the EDA findings, separating row-dropping rules from capping/clipping rules.
  2. Apply row-dropping rules to train only -- the test set has no label to justify a drop, and every test row must still receive a prediction.
  3. Apply capping/clipping rules identically to train and test, using bounds derived from train only.

C. Preprocessing¶

  1. Split features (X) and target (y) from the cleaned training set.
  2. Build a preprocessing pipeline (encoders/scalers appropriate to each feature type).
  3. Fit simple transformers on the training features only; if any encoder uses target information, fit it out-of-fold to avoid leakage.
  4. Transform the training features.
  5. Transform the held-out validation split and the test features using the transformer(s) fit on train only.

D. Model¶

  1. Establish a naive baseline to contextualize later scores.
  2. Train candidate models and compare via cross-validation on the competition metric.
  3. Tune hyperparameters of the best candidate.
  4. Refit the final model on the full cleaned training set.
  5. Evaluate on a held-out split to check for systematic error patterns.
  6. Predict on the test set, format the submission, and sanity-check the predicted distribution against train.

1. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

This section explores the dataset in depth before any modelling takes place, moving through four phases: understanding the raw data, checking it for quality issues, exploring feature-target relationships, and summarising the findings.

1.1 Understand¶

This section establishes what the raw data looks like: its structure, feature groups, and how the modelling matrix is assembled.

First step is to load the required libraries and load the data (The libraries has been appended after each stage).

from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd


DATA_DIR = Path("../datasets")

TRAIN_VALUES_FILE = DATA_DIR / "train_values.csv"
TRAIN_LABELS_FILE = DATA_DIR / "train_labels.csv"
TEST_VALUES_FILE = DATA_DIR / "test_values.csv"


def load_data(data_dir: Path):
    """Load train_values, train_labels, and test_values from data_dir."""
    
    files = {
        "train_values": data_dir / "train_values.csv",
        "train_labels": data_dir / "train_labels.csv",
        "test_values": data_dir / "test_values.csv",
    }

    missing = [str(p) for p in files.values() if not p.exists()]

    if missing:
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"Expected data file(s) not found: {missing}. "
            f"Pass the correct folder with --data-dir."
        )

    train_values = pd.read_csv(files["train_values"])
    train_labels = pd.read_csv(files["train_labels"])
    test_values = pd.read_csv(files["test_values"])

    return train_values, train_labels, test_values


train_values, train_labels, test_values = load_data(DATA_DIR)

print("Data loaded successfully!")

Data loaded successfully!

1.1.2 Feature Groups¶

The dataset contains several types of variables:

  • Geographic identifiers
  • Continuous/count variables
  • Categorical building characteristics
  • Binary structural-material indicators
  • Binary secondary-use indicators

The geographic IDs are treated as categorical variables by LightGBM because their numeric values represent geographic identifiers rather than continuous measurements.

1.1.4 Dataset Shapes and Key Alignment¶

The checks below confirm that:

  • The number of training observations matches the number of labels.
  • Building IDs are unique within each dataset.
  • Training and test feature schemas are consistent apart from the training target.

Interpretation

  • Train values (260,601 x 39), train labels (260,601 x 2) and test values (86,868 x 39) all have unique building_ids, and the assertion checks confirm a clean 1:1 alignment between features and labels with no orphan or duplicate IDs.
  • The test set is roughly a third of the size of the training set (86,868 vs 260,601 rows), and both share an identical feature schema apart from the training-only target column.
  • This is a data-integrity check rather than a feature/damage-grade relationship, but it guarantees that every downstream merge between train_values and train_labels (used throughout the rest of the EDA) is safe and leak-free.

1.2 Clean¶

This section addresses data-quality issues -- missing values, duplicate rows, and invalid or sentinel values -- that could affect modelling.

1.2.1 Missing Values¶

Missing values can affect both preprocessing and model training, so we inspect every dataset before proceeding.

In [45]:

    "train_labels": train_labels.isna().sum(),
    "test_values": test_values.isna().sum(),
})

missing_summary = missing_summary.fillna(0).astype(int)

missing_summary[missing_summary.sum(axis=1) > 0]

print("Test values :", test_values.isna().sum().sum())

Total missing values
Train values: 0
Train labels: 0
Test values : 0

Interpretation

  • Zero missing values were found in train_values, train_labels, and test_values.
  • The dataset is complete-case, so no imputation strategy is required and every categorical/numeric/binary feature can be used as-is when it is later related to damage_grade without missingness distorting any of the group statistics computed later in the EDA.

1.2.2 Duplicate Rows¶

Two types of duplication are checked:

  1. Fully duplicated rows.
  2. Duplicated feature rows after removing building_id.

A duplicated feature row does not automatically mean that the observations should be removed. Multiple buildings can legitimately share the same recorded characteristics.

In [46]:
full_duplicates = train_values.duplicated().sum()

feature_duplicates = (
    train_values.drop(columns=[ID_COL])
    .duplicated()
    .sum()
)

print(f"Fully duplicated rows      : {full_duplicates:,}")
print(f"Duplicated feature rows    : {feature_duplicates:,}")

Fully duplicated rows      : 0
Duplicated feature rows    : 16,191

Interpretation

  • There are 0 fully duplicated rows (expected, since building_id is unique per row), but 16,191 rows (~6.2% of the 260,601 training buildings) share identical feature values once building_id is dropped.
  • This reflects the low cardinality of most categorical/binary features rather than a data-quality problem: many buildings genuinely share the same foundation type, roof type, floor materials, and geographic location, which is plausible in areas with repeated/standardised construction styles.
  • These rows are not removed, since doing so would arbitrarily discard real observations and could shift the damage-grade distribution for common building typologies.

1.2.3 Invalid / Sentinel Values (Age)¶

The age feature is checked for sentinel/placeholder values that could distort scale-sensitive models.

In [47]:
bins = [-1, 9, 19, 29, 39, 49, 59, 69, 79, 89, 99, 149, 199, 994, 995]
labels = [f"{x}-{x+9}" for x in range(0, 100, 10)] + ["100-149", "150-199", "200-994", "995"]

age_pct = (
    pd.cut(X["age"], bins=bins, labels=labels, include_lowest=True)
    .value_counts(sort=False)
    .div(len(X))
    .mul(100)
)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
bars = plt.bar(age_pct.index.astype(str), age_pct)

plt.title("Building Age Distribution")
plt.xlabel("Building Age (years)")
plt.ylabel("Percentage of Buildings (%)")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)

for bar, pct in zip(bars, age_pct):
    if pct:
        plt.text(
            bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
            bar.get_height(),
            f"{pct:.1f}%",
            ha="center",
            va="bottom",
            fontsize=9
        )

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation

  • The distribution is heavily right-skewed and dominated by young buildings: ages 0-39 account for ~84% of the dataset (0-9: 22.9%, 10-19: 28.7%, 20-29: 21.7%, 30-39: 11.0%), and each successive decade bucket keeps shrinking through the 90s.
  • The custom bins isolate the anomaly cleanly: the 150-199 and 200-994 buckets are essentially empty (0.1% and 0.0%), yet the chart jumps back up to 0.5% exactly at the 995 bin — a discontinuity that would not occur if 995 were a genuine continuation of the age distribution.
  • 1,390 buildings (0.533%) have age == 995, and 1,496 buildings (0.574%) have age >= 200 — meaning almost all unusually old ages (1,390 of 1,496) are exactly 995, with only ~106 buildings holding a genuinely large-but-plausible age between 200 and 994.
  • This pattern strongly suggests 995 is a sentinel/placeholder code (e.g. "unknown" or "very old") rather than a literal building age, and it should be treated as a special category rather than a continuous value in any scale-sensitive model — tree-based models such as LightGBM/XGBoost handle this gracefully since a sentinel value simply becomes a valid split point, which is one reason boosting methods suit this dataset well.

1.3 Explore¶

With data-quality issues identified, we explore feature distributions and their relationship with the target variable.

1.3.1 Target Distribution¶

The target distribution is important because the three damage grades are not equally represented.

Both absolute counts and percentages are examined before evaluating models.

In [48]:

    target_summary["count"]

    target_summary["count"],
    labels=[f"Grade {i}" for i in target_summary.index],
    autopct="%1.0f%%",
    startangle=90

axes[1].set_title("Damage Grade Distribution")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation

  • The target is imbalanced: Grade 1 (low damage) is a minority at 9.64% (25,124 buildings), Grade 2 (medium damage) dominates at 56.89% (148,259), and Grade 3 (near-total destruction) makes up 33.47% (87,218).
  • Because Micro-F1 is equivalent to accuracy for this single-label problem, a naive "always predict Grade 2" baseline would already score ~56.9%, so this class imbalance alone could make accuracy-style metrics look deceptively high without the Low- and Severe-damage classes being distinguished well.
  • Given this skew, Macro-F1 is a useful diagnostic metric alongside Micro-F1 for judging performance on the minority Grade 1 class — since the competition's official evaluation metric is Micro-F1 (equivalent to accuracy here), Macro-F1 should supplement rather than replace it when tracking model performance. Any train/validation split would probably need to be stratified to keep class proportions consistent across both sets.

1.3.2 Geographic Features¶

The three geographic variables form a nested hierarchy:

  • geo_level_1_id
  • geo_level_2_id
  • geo_level_3_id

They are identifiers rather than continuous measurements, so their cardinality and relationship with damage grade are more informative than their numeric values themselves.

import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go


# =========================================================
# Stratified-looking geographic sample
# =========================================================

GEO_SAMPLE_SIZE = 5000

geo_data = X[
    [
        "geo_level_1_id",
        "geo_level_2_id",
        "geo_level_3_id"
    ]
].copy()

# Calculate proportional sample size for each Geo 1 → Geo 2 group
group_sizes = (
    geo_data
    .groupby(
        ["geo_level_1_id", "geo_level_2_id"]
    )
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="count")
)

group_sizes["sample_n"] = (
    group_sizes["count"]
    .div(len(geo_data))
    .mul(GEO_SAMPLE_SIZE)
    .round()
    .astype(int)
    .clip(lower=1)
)

sampled_groups = []

for _, group in group_sizes.iterrows():

    mask = (
        (geo_data["geo_level_1_id"] == group["geo_level_1_id"]) &
        (geo_data["geo_level_2_id"] == group["geo_level_2_id"])
    )

    group_data = geo_data.loc[mask]

    sampled_groups.append(
        group_data.sample(
            n=min(group["sample_n"], len(group_data)),
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE
        )
    )

geo_sample = (
    pd.concat(sampled_groups)
    .sample(
        n=min(GEO_SAMPLE_SIZE, len(pd.concat(sampled_groups))),
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE
    )
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

geo_sample = geo_sample.astype(str)

# =========================================================
# 2. Count observations at each hierarchy level
# =========================================================

geo1 = (
    geo_sample
    .groupby("geo_level_1_id")
    .size()
)

geo2 = (
    geo_sample
    .groupby(
        ["geo_level_1_id", "geo_level_2_id"]
    )
    .size()
)

geo3 = (
    geo_sample
    .groupby(
        [
            "geo_level_1_id",
            "geo_level_2_id",
            "geo_level_3_id"
        ]
    )
    .size()
)


# =========================================================
# 3. Build sunburst nodes
# =========================================================

ids = []
labels = []
parents = []
values = []
hover_text = []


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Geo Level 1
# ---------------------------------------------------------

for geo1_id, count in geo1.items():

    node_id = f"geo1_{geo1_id}"

    ids.append(node_id)
    labels.append(f"geo_level_1_id = {geo1_id}")
    parents.append("")
    values.append(count)

    hover_text.append(
        f"<b>geo_level_1_id = {geo1_id}</b>"
        f"<br>Buildings in sample: {count}"
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Geo Level 2
# ---------------------------------------------------------

for (geo1_id, geo2_id), count in geo2.items():

    node_id = f"geo2_{geo1_id}_{geo2_id}"
    parent_id = f"geo1_{geo1_id}"

    ids.append(node_id)
    labels.append(f"geo_level_2_id = {geo2_id}")
    parents.append(parent_id)
    values.append(count)

    hover_text.append(
        f"<b>geo_level_2_id = {geo2_id}</b>"
        f"<br>geo_level_1_id = {geo1_id}"
        f"<br>Buildings in sample: {count}"
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Geo Level 3
# ---------------------------------------------------------

for (
    geo1_id,
    geo2_id,
    geo3_id
), count in geo3.items():

    node_id = (
        f"geo3_{geo1_id}_{geo2_id}_{geo3_id}"
    )

    parent_id = (
        f"geo2_{geo1_id}_{geo2_id}"
    )

    ids.append(node_id)
    labels.append(f"geo_level_3_id = {geo3_id}")
    parents.append(parent_id)
    values.append(count)

    hover_text.append(
        f"<b>geo_level_3_id = {geo3_id}</b>"
        f"<br>geo_level_2_id = {geo2_id}"
        f"<br>geo_level_1_id = {geo1_id}"
        f"<br>Buildings in sample: {count}"
    )


# =========================================================
# 4. Create figure
# =========================================================

fig = go.Figure(
    go.Sunburst(
        ids=ids,
        labels=labels,
        parents=parents,
        values=values,
        branchvalues="total",
        customdata=hover_text,
        hovertemplate=(
            "%{customdata}"
            "<extra></extra>"
        )
    )
)


# =========================================================
# 5. Layout
# =========================================================

fig.update_layout(
    title=(
        "Geographic Hierarchy: "
        "Geo Level 1 → Geo Level 2 → Geo Level 3"
    ),
    width=950,
    height=850,
    margin=dict(
        t=80,
        l=20,
        r=20,
        b=20
    )
)

fig.show()

Interpretation

  • Cardinality increases sharply down the geographic hierarchy: geo_level_1_id has 31 unique values, geo_level_2_id has 1,414, and geo_level_3_id has 11,595 — roughly a 45x and 8x increase at each finer level.
  • The hierarchy-check confirms the three levels are perfectly nested (0 geo_level_3_ids map to more than one geo_level_2_id parent, and 0 geo_level_2_ids map to more than one geo_level_1_id parent), so each finer geographic ID uniquely rolls up into a single coarser region.
  • This nesting matters for the damage-grade relationship uncovered later: geo_level_3_id turns out to be the single strongest predictor of damage_grade in both the association (Cramér's V 0.555) and mutual-information analyses, and even the coarse geo_level_1_id alone reaches 0.373 — location captures shaking intensity, soil conditions, and local construction practice, which appears to dominate the damage outcome more than any individual building attribute.

Interpretation

  • Severe-damage (Grade 3) share varies enormously across the 31 geo_level_1_id regions — from roughly 8-9% in the safest regions (e.g. ids 26, 5, 29) up to roughly 75-80% in the hardest-hit regions (ids 17, 18), a nearly 10x range.
  • This spread is far wider than anything seen among the individual categorical or numeric building features, which is why geo_level_1_id alone already reaches a Cramér's V of 0.373, rising to 0.555 for the more granular geo_level_3_id.
  • It strongly suggests that regional differences in earthquake shaking intensity, soil conditions, and/or local construction standards are the dominant driver of damage outcomes in this dataset — more so than any single building-level attribute.

1.3.3 Numeric Feature Summary¶

The distributions and summary statistics of the continuous/count variables are inspected below.

Special attention is given to age, where unusually large values may represent special survey codes rather than realistic building ages.

Interpretation

  • count_floors_pre_eq is tightly distributed (mean 2.13, std 0.73, range 1-9), with most buildings having 2 floors.
  • area_percentage (mean 8.0, range 1-100) and height_percentage (mean 5.4, range 2-32) are both right-skewed footprint/height proxies.
  • count_families is almost always exactly 1 (mean 0.98, std 0.42, range 0-9), meaning it carries very little variance to explain damage outcomes.
  • age stands out: the mean (26.5) is far above the median (15), and the max (995) is wildly inconsistent with the 75th percentile (30), signalling a heavy right skew driven by extreme outliers.

In [55]:
def categorical_damage_analysis(df, target, feature):
    """Plot category prevalence and damage-grade distribution."""

    # Category prevalence
    value_pct = (
        df[feature]
        .value_counts(normalize=True)
        .sort_values(ascending=False) * 100
    )
    category_order = value_pct.index

    # Damage-grade distribution
    damage_pct = (
        pd.crosstab(df[feature], target, normalize="index") * 100
    ).reindex(
        index=category_order,
        columns=[1, 2, 3],
        fill_value=0
    )

    # Plot
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 5))

    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    # Category prevalence
    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    value_pct.plot(kind="barh", ax=axes[0])
    axes[0].invert_yaxis()

    for bar in axes[0].patches:
        width = bar.get_width()
        y = bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2

        axes[0].text(
            width / 2 if width > 5 else width + 0.3,
            y,
            f"{width:.1f}%",
            ha="center" if width > 5 else "left",
            va="center",
            fontsize=9,
            fontweight="bold",
            color="black"
        )

    axes[0].set_title(f"{feature} — Category Prevalence")
    axes[0].set_xlabel("Percentage of Buildings")
    axes[0].set_ylabel(feature)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    # Damage-grade distribution
    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    damage_colors = ["#D8B08C", "#C85A54", "#8B0000"]

    damage_pct.plot(
        kind="barh",
        stacked=True,
        ax=axes[1],
        color=damage_colors
    )
    axes[1].invert_yaxis()

    for bar in axes[1].patches:
        width = bar.get_width()

        if width >= 3:
            axes[1].text(
                bar.get_x() + width / 2,
                bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2,
                f"{width:.1f}%",
                ha="center",
                va="center",
                fontsize=9,
                fontweight="bold",
                color="black"
            )

    axes[1].set_title(f"{feature} — Damage Grade Distribution")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("Percentage within Category")
    axes[1].set_ylabel(feature)

    axes[1].legend(
        title="Damage Grade",
        loc="upper left",
        bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1)
    )

    plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 0.90, 1])
    plt.show()

    return value_pct, damage_pct

1.3.5 Binary Structural and Secondary-Use Features¶

Binary indicators describe structural materials and secondary building use.

This covers:

  • Prevalence of superstructure materials
  • Prevalence of secondary-use categories
  • Number of superstructure flags set per building
  • Damage distribution across geographic regions

prevalence = (
    X[SUPERSTRUCTURE_COLS]
    .mean()
    .mul(100)
    .sort_values()
)

damage = (
    X[SUPERSTRUCTURE_COLS]
    .assign(damage_grade=y.values)
    .melt(
        "damage_grade",
        var_name="superstructure",
        value_name="present"
    )
    .query("present == 1")
    .groupby(["superstructure", "damage_grade"])
    .size()
    .groupby(level=0)
    .transform(lambda x: x / x.sum() * 100)
    .rename("percentage")
    .reset_index()
    .pivot(
        index="superstructure",
        columns="damage_grade",
        values="percentage"
    )
    .fillna(0)
    .reindex(prevalence.index)
)

  • Because a building can carry multiple superstructure flags, this reflects a construction landscape heavily weighted toward informal/traditional materials and only lightly toward earthquake-resistant engineered concrete — consistent with the overall skew toward Grade 2/3 damage seen in the target distribution.
  • has_superstructure_mud_mortar_stone has the highest association with damage_grade of any binary indicator, so its very high prevalence is a major contributor to the dataset's damage outcomes.

  • Despite this rarity, has_secondary_use_hotel (0.108) and has_secondary_use_rental (0.101) still appear in the top-15 association ranking later in the EDA — this is more likely a proxy effect (hotels/rentals concentrated in specific geographic areas or building types) than a direct causal link between secondary use and structural damage.

1.3.6 Numeric Features and Damage Grade¶

The distributions of numeric variables are compared across the three damage grades.

This helps identify variables for which the distribution shifts systematically with increasing damage severity.

Interpretation

  • age shows the clearest ordinal relationship: median age rises monotonically with damage severity (Grade 1 median 5 -> Grade 2 median 15 -> Grade 3 median 20), i.e. older buildings trend toward more severe damage.
  • count_floors_pre_eq has the same median (2) across all three grades, but Grade 3 has a visibly wider spread (IQR extending to 3, whisker to 4 floors) compared to Grade 1 (whisker to 3), suggesting taller buildings are over-represented among severe-damage cases.
  • height_percentage is flat at a median of 5 for every grade, but again Grade 3's IQR (5-7) sits above Grade 1's (3-6), a mild version of the same "taller buildings skew toward more damage" pattern.
  • area_percentage shows only a weak, non-monotonic shift (median 8 for Grade 1 vs 7 for Grade 2 and Grade 3).
  • count_families is constant at a median of 1 across all grades, carrying essentially no signal — consistent with it being almost always exactly 1 family per building (from the earlier describe table).
  • Overall, age and count_floors_pre_eq are the most informative numeric features, but all five numeric variables rank below the geographic and structural-material features in both the association test (max |Pearson r| 0.125 for area_percentage) and mutual information analyses later in the EDA.

1.3.7 Correlation and Collinearity¶

Pearson correlation is meaningful for continuous/count variables and binary indicators, but not for categorical labels or geographic IDs.

The correlation matrix therefore uses only the numeric and binary features.

Pairs with absolute correlation above 0.80 are flagged as a simple collinearity screening rule. This is a diagnostic threshold rather than an automatic feature-removal rule.

No feature pairs have an absolute correlation greater than or equal to 0.80.

Interpretation

  • The heatmap's brightest off-diagonal cell is count_floors_pre_eq vs height_percentage (a naturally expected positive relationship, since more floors generally means a taller building), and has_secondary_use vs has_secondary_use_agriculture / has_secondary_use_hotel are also elevated, since the umbrella flag is set whenever any sub-flag is.
  • The darkest (most negative) cells are among the superstructure material flags — e.g. has_superstructure_mud_mortar_stone vs has_superstructure_cement_mortar_brick — reflecting that these are largely mutually exclusive construction choices (a building built with one material is less likely to also use a competing one) rather than true redundancy.
  • The explicit check confirms no feature pair reaches |correlation| >= 0.80, so no numeric/binary features need to be dropped for collinearity before modelling — all of them can be retained, which particularly matters for the linear/logistic baseline.

1.3.8 Feature Association with Damage Grade¶

Different feature types require different association measures:

  • Categorical and binary variables → Cramér's V
  • Continuous/count variables → absolute Pearson correlation

Geographic IDs are treated as categorical variables because their numerical values are identifiers rather than continuous quantities.

In [70]:
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency


def cramers_v(x, y):
    """Calculate Cramér's V for two categorical variables."""

    confusion = pd.crosstab(x, y)

    chi2 = chi2_contingency(confusion)[0]

    n = confusion.sum().sum()
    phi2 = chi2 / n

    r, k = confusion.shape

    phi2_corrected = max(
        0,
        phi2 - ((k - 1) * (r - 1)) / (n - 1)
    )

    r_corrected = (
        r
        - ((r - 1) ** 2) / (n - 1)
    )

    k_corrected = (
        k
        - ((k - 1) ** 2) / (n - 1)
    )

    denominator = min(
        k_corrected - 1,
        r_corrected - 1
    )

    if denominator <= 0:
        return 0.0

    return np.sqrt(phi2_corrected / denominator)

1.3.9 Mutual Information¶

Mutual information measures the dependency between each feature and the target.

Unlike Pearson correlation, it can capture nonlinear relationships.

Categorical, geographic, and binary variables are treated as discrete variables; continuous/count variables are treated as continuous.

In [73]:

    discrete_features.append(col not in NUMERIC_COLS)

    mi_input,
    y,
    discrete_features=discrete_features,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,

    "Feature": ALL_FEATURE_COLS,
    "Mutual Information": mi_scores,
})

Interpretation

  • Mutual information corroborates the association ranking from Section 1.3.8: the same top three features are the geographic IDs (geo_level_3_id 0.334, geo_level_2_id 0.240, geo_level_1_id 0.132), followed by the same structural-material/type tier (foundation_type 0.071, ground_floor_type 0.054, has_superstructure_mud_mortar_stone 0.049, other_floor_type 0.048, roof_type 0.041).
  • Agreement between Cramér's V/Pearson (Section 1.3.8) and mutual information here is useful because MI can capture non-linear relationships that chi-square/Pearson-based measures might miss — the fact that both methods agree on the same top features increases confidence that this ranking is a genuine data pattern rather than an artifact of either measure's assumptions.
  • A long tail of features — most secondary-use flags, land_surface_condition, plan_configuration, position, legal_ownership_status, and most individual superstructure flags — carry essentially zero mutual information (<=0.003) with damage_grade, marking them as the weakest individual predictors and the first candidates to de-prioritise if feature selection is needed, while the geographic IDs and core structural-material/type features should be prioritised in any downstream model.

1.4 Summarise¶

The EDA highlights several important characteristics of the problem:

  1. The target is imbalanced, with Grade 2 representing the largest class.
  2. Geographic variables are highly informative, with increasingly fine geographic levels providing substantial information about damage grade.
  3. Foundation and structural-material variables show strong associations with damage severity.
  4. Building age is informative, although the value 995 should be treated carefully because it appears to represent a special survey value rather than an ordinary building age.
  5. Categorical and binary structural features contain substantial predictive information.
  6. The geographic variables are identifiers, so their numerical values should not be interpreted as measurements.
  7. The combination of categorical, binary, geographic and numeric variables makes tree-based boosting methods particularly suitable for this problem.

2. Cleaning¶

Based on the EDA findings above, no rows required dropping and no capping/clipping rules were necessary; the raw feature values are passed through to preprocessing and modelling.

2.1 Feature Engineering¶

Several derived features are added before the train/validation split. These target two things the raw 38 columns don't capture well:

  1. Structural and age signal that isn't explicit in any single column -- mixed-material construction, building slenderness, occupant density, and the age == 995 survey placeholder (Section 1.2.3) get their own explicit features instead of being left for the model to infer from raw columns.
  2. The sparsity of geo_level_3_id -- 11,595 distinct regions, median ~14 buildings each, and 20% with 3 or fewer buildings (Section 1.3.2). Passed in raw, LightGBM/CatBoost can still overfit these tiny buckets. A frequency count is added here (leakage-free -- it only uses id density, not the target); a hierarchical smoothed target encoding is added later, right after the train/validation split, so it can be fit without ever seeing the target of a row it's about to encode.

These are pure feature transforms -- no target is used in this cell -- so they're computed once and applied identically to X and X_test.

In [ ]:
def engineer_features(df, geo2_count_map=None, geo3_count_map=None):
    """Pure feature transforms -- no target used, safe to apply to train and test alike."""

    df = df.copy()

    # age == 995 is a survey placeholder (EDA 1.2.3), not a real building age --
    # flag it explicitly instead of letting the model treat it as "very old".
    df["age_is_placeholder"] = (df["age"] == 995).astype(int)
    df["age_bucket"] = pd.cut(
        df["age"],
        bins=[-1, 5, 15, 30, 994, 10_000],
        labels=["new", "moderate", "old", "very_old", "unknown"],
    ).astype(str)

    df["age_x_floors"] = df["age"] * df["count_floors_pre_eq"]
    df["height_area_ratio"] = df["height_percentage"] / df["area_percentage"].clip(lower=1)
    df["family_density"] = df["count_families"] / df["count_floors_pre_eq"].clip(lower=1)

    # How many distinct superstructure materials / secondary uses a building reports --
    # mixed-material construction behaves differently from single-material.
    df["superstructure_material_count"] = df[SUPERSTRUCTURE_COLS].sum(axis=1)
    df["secondary_use_count"] = df[SECONDARY_USE_SUB_COLS].sum(axis=1)

    df["foundation_position"] = (
        df["foundation_type"].astype(str) + "_" + df["position"].astype(str)
    )

    # Frequency (density) of each geo region -- fit on training ids only, mapped onto
    # both train and test; unseen ids (327 geo3, 5 geo2 rows in test) get 0.
    if geo2_count_map is not None:
        df["geo2_count"] = df["geo_level_2_id"].map(geo2_count_map).fillna(0).astype(int)
    if geo3_count_map is not None:
        df["geo3_count"] = df["geo_level_3_id"].map(geo3_count_map).fillna(0).astype(int)

    return df


class GeoHierarchicalTargetEncoder:
    """Encode geographic IDs using smoothed damage rates from their parent regions.
    Small regions borrow information from larger regions to make the encoding more reliable.
    """

    def __init__(self, smoothing=(20, 40, 20)):
        self.smoothing = smoothing

    def fit(self, X, y):
        y = pd.Series(np.asarray(y, dtype=float), index=X.index)
        s1, s2, s3 = self.smoothing
        global_mean = y.mean()

        geo2_parent = X.groupby("geo_level_2_id")["geo_level_1_id"].first()
        geo3_parent = X.groupby("geo_level_3_id")["geo_level_2_id"].first()

        agg1 = y.groupby(X["geo_level_1_id"]).agg(["mean", "count"])
        geo1_map = (agg1["mean"] * agg1["count"] + global_mean * s1) / (agg1["count"] + s1)

        agg2 = y.groupby(X["geo_level_2_id"]).agg(["mean", "count"])
        parent2_mean = geo2_parent.map(geo1_map).fillna(global_mean)
        geo2_map = (agg2["mean"] * agg2["count"] + parent2_mean * s2) / (agg2["count"] + s2)

        agg3 = y.groupby(X["geo_level_3_id"]).agg(["mean", "count"])
        parent3_mean = geo3_parent.map(geo2_map).fillna(global_mean)
        geo3_map = (agg3["mean"] * agg3["count"] + parent3_mean * s3) / (agg3["count"] + s3)

        self.global_mean_ = global_mean
        self.geo1_map_, self.geo2_map_, self.geo3_map_ = geo1_map, geo2_map, geo3_map
        self.geo2_parent_, self.geo3_parent_ = geo2_parent, geo3_parent
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        geo1_te = X["geo_level_1_id"].map(self.geo1_map_).fillna(self.global_mean_)

        geo2_fallback = X["geo_level_1_id"].map(self.geo1_map_).fillna(self.global_mean_)
        geo2_te = X["geo_level_2_id"].map(self.geo2_map_).fillna(geo2_fallback)

        geo3_fallback = X["geo_level_2_id"].map(self.geo2_map_).fillna(geo2_fallback)
        geo3_te = X["geo_level_3_id"].map(self.geo3_map_).fillna(geo3_fallback)

        return pd.DataFrame(
            {"geo1_te": geo1_te, "geo2_te": geo2_te, "geo3_te": geo3_te},
            index=X.index,
        )

    def fit_transform(self, X, y):
        return self.fit(X, y).transform(X)

3. Preprocessing¶

Feature encoding and scaling are built as part of each model's pipeline in Section 4, fitted on the training split only. This section covers the train/validation split itself.

3.1 Train/Validation Split¶

A stratified 80/20 split is used so that the validation set preserves approximately the same damage-grade proportions as the complete training data.

This validation set will be used consistently to compare the baseline models.

In [77]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


X_train, X_valid, y_train, y_valid = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.20,
    stratify=y,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

print("Training set  :", X_train.shape)
print("Validation set:", X_valid.shape)

print("\nTraining target distribution:")
print(y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index())

print("\nValidation target distribution:")
print(y_valid.value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index())

3.2 Geo Hierarchical Target Encoding¶

geo1_te / geo2_te / geo3_te are added here -- fit on X_train/y_train only, then applied to both X_train and X_valid -- so every baseline model from this point on sees them. Fitting after the split (rather than in Section 2.1) is what keeps this leakage-free: the encoder never sees the target of a row it's about to encode.

In [78]:
geo_encoder = GeoHierarchicalTargetEncoder(smoothing=(20, 40, 20))
geo_encoder.fit(X_train, y_train)

X_train[["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]] = geo_encoder.transform(X_train)
X_valid[["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]] = geo_encoder.transform(X_valid)

NUMERIC_COLS = NUMERIC_COLS + ["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]

print(f"NUMERIC_COLS now includes geo_te columns ({len(NUMERIC_COLS)} total).")
print(X_train[["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]].describe())

4. Model¶

Baseline models are trained and compared, the best candidate is tuned, and the final model is used to generate predictions for submission.

4.1 Model Evaluation¶

All classification models will be evaluated on exactly the same validation set.

The following metrics are recorded:

  • Micro-F1 — primary evaluation metric
  • Accuracy
  • Macro-F1 — useful for understanding performance across classes
  • Weighted-F1 — accounts for class frequency

For this single-label multiclass problem, Micro-F1 and Accuracy are mathematically equivalent.

In [79]:
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    classification_report,
    confusion_matrix,
    f1_score,
)


validation_results = []


def evaluate_model(model_name, y_true, y_pred):
    """Evaluate a multiclass classifier and store validation metrics."""

    metrics = {
        "Model": model_name,
        "Micro-F1": f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average="micro"),
        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
        "Macro-F1": f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average="macro"),
        "Weighted-F1": f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average="weighted"),
    }

    validation_results.append(metrics)

    print(f"\n{model_name}")
    print("-" * len(model_name))
    print(f"Micro-F1    : {metrics['Micro-F1']:.4f}")
    print(f"Accuracy    : {metrics['Accuracy']:.4f}")
    print(f"Macro-F1    : {metrics['Macro-F1']:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted-F1 : {metrics['Weighted-F1']:.4f}")

    print("\nClassification report:")
    print(
        classification_report(
            y_true,
            y_pred,
            digits=4
        )
    )

    return metrics

4.2 Logistic Regression Baseline¶

Logistic Regression provides a simple linear baseline.

Categorical and geographic features are one-hot encoded, continuous variables are standardized, and binary indicators are passed through unchanged.

class_weight="balanced" is used because the damage grades are imbalanced.

In [80]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler


logistic_preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("numeric", StandardScaler(), NUMERIC_COLS),
        (
            "categorical",
            OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"),
            CATEGORICAL_COLS,
        ),
        (
            "geo",
            OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"),
            GEO_COLS,
        ),
        ("binary", "passthrough", BINARY_COLS),
    ],
    remainder="drop",
)


logistic_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("preprocessor", logistic_preprocessor),
        (
            "classifier",
            LogisticRegression(
                max_iter=1000,
                class_weight="balanced",
                random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
            ),
        ),
    ]
)


logistic_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

logistic_pred = logistic_pipeline.predict(X_valid)

evaluate_model(
    "Logistic Regression",
    y_valid,
    logistic_pred
)

4.3 Random Forest Baseline¶

4.4 XGBoost Baseline¶

XGBoost is evaluated as a second gradient-boosted tree benchmark.

To keep the comparison focused, this notebook uses a single predefined multiclass configuration rather than performing a separate hyperparameter search.

Categorical variables are encoded numerically using OrdinalEncoder. The resulting feature matrix is suitable for XGBoost's tree-based learner.

In [82]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder


xgb_preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        (
            "categorical",
            OrdinalEncoder(
                handle_unknown="use_encoded_value",
                unknown_value=-1,
            ),
            [*GEO_COLS, *CATEGORICAL_COLS],
        ),
        ("numeric", "passthrough", NUMERIC_COLS),
        ("binary", "passthrough", BINARY_COLS),
    ],
    remainder="drop",
)
In [83]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder
from xgboost import XGBClassifier


# XGBoost requires class labels to start at 0.
# Original damage grades are 1, 2, 3.
xgb_label_map = {
    1: 0,
    2: 1,
    3: 2,
}

xgb_inverse_label_map = {
    0: 1,
    1: 2,
    2: 3,
}

y_train_xgb = y_train.map(xgb_label_map)
y_valid_xgb = y_valid.map(xgb_label_map)


xgb_preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        (
            "categorical",
            OrdinalEncoder(
                handle_unknown="use_encoded_value",
                unknown_value=-1,
            ),
            [*GEO_COLS, *CATEGORICAL_COLS],
        ),
        ("numeric", "passthrough", NUMERIC_COLS),
        ("binary", "passthrough", BINARY_COLS),
    ],
    remainder="drop",
)


xgb_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("preprocessor", xgb_preprocessor),
        (
            "classifier",
            XGBClassifier(
                objective="multi:softmax",
                num_class=3,
                n_estimators=500,
                learning_rate=0.05,
                max_depth=6,
                min_child_weight=5,
                subsample=0.8,
                colsample_bytree=0.8,
                random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
                n_jobs=-1,
                eval_metric="mlogloss",
                tree_method="hist",
            ),
        ),
    ]
)


xgb_pipeline.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train_xgb,
)


# XGBoost returns 0, 1, 2.
# Convert back to the original damage grades 1, 2, 3.
xgb_pred_encoded = xgb_pipeline.predict(X_valid)

xgb_pred = pd.Series(
    xgb_pred_encoded,
    index=y_valid.index,
).map(xgb_inverse_label_map)


evaluate_model(
    "XGBoost",
    y_valid,
    xgb_pred,
)

4.5 LightGBM Baseline¶

LightGBM is particularly suitable for this dataset because it can directly handle categorical variables and efficiently model nonlinear interactions.

The three geographic identifiers are treated as categorical variables because they are hierarchical region IDs rather than continuous measurements.

In [84]:
import lightgbm as lgb


LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS = [
    *GEO_COLS,
    *CATEGORICAL_COLS,
]


def prepare_lgb_data(train_df, valid_df=None, categorical_cols=None):
    """Convert categorical columns to aligned pandas categorical dtype."""

    categorical_cols = categorical_cols or []

    train_out = train_df.copy()
    valid_out = None if valid_df is None else valid_df.copy()

    for col in categorical_cols:
        train_out[col] = train_out[col].astype("category")

        if valid_out is not None:
            valid_out[col] = valid_out[col].astype("category")
            valid_out[col] = valid_out[col].cat.set_categories(
                train_out[col].cat.categories
            )

    return train_out, valid_out
In [85]:
X_train_lgb, X_valid_lgb = prepare_lgb_data(
    X_train,
    X_valid,
    LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
)


lgb_baseline = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    objective="multiclass",
    num_class=3,
    n_estimators=500,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    num_leaves=31,
    max_depth=-1,
    subsample=0.8,
    subsample_freq=1,
    colsample_bytree=0.8,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
    force_col_wise=True,
    verbosity=-1,
)


lgb_baseline.fit(
    X_train_lgb,
    y_train,
    categorical_feature=LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS,
)


lgb_baseline_pred = lgb_baseline.predict(X_valid_lgb).astype(int)

evaluate_model(
    "LightGBM Baseline",
    y_valid,
    lgb_baseline_pred
)

4.5b CatBoost Baseline¶

CatBoost is tried alongside LightGBM because its ordered target statistics are effectively a leakage-safe smoothed target encoding built into the algorithm for exactly the high-cardinality, sparse categoricals this dataset has (geo_level_3_id especially). Raw geo/categorical columns are passed in unmodified via cat_features -- no separate encoding step needed.

In [86]:
from catboost import CatBoostClassifier


CAT_FEATURES = [*GEO_COLS, *CATEGORICAL_COLS]


catboost_baseline = CatBoostClassifier(
    loss_function="MultiClass",
    iterations=500,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    depth=6,
    l2_leaf_reg=3,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    thread_count=-1,
    verbose=False,
)

catboost_baseline.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cat_features=CAT_FEATURES,
)

catboost_baseline_pred = (
    catboost_baseline.predict(X_valid).astype(int).ravel()
)

evaluate_model(
    "CatBoost Baseline",
    y_valid,
    catboost_baseline_pred,
)

4.7 LightGBM Hyperparameter Tuning¶

Rather than performing a very large hyperparameter search, this uses RandomizedSearchCV over a deliberately narrow range based on the behaviour observed during model development.

The search focuses on:

  • num_leaves
  • min_child_samples
  • colsample_bytree
  • subsample

The learning rate and number of estimators are kept fixed to control the search space.

The search itself uses stratified 3-fold cross-validation and Micro-F1 as the optimization metric.

In [88]:
from sklearn.metrics import make_scorer
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV, StratifiedKFold


micro_f1_scorer = make_scorer(
    f1_score,
    average="micro"
)


lgb_search_model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    objective="multiclass",
    num_class=3,
    n_estimators=900,
    learning_rate=0.03,
    max_depth=-1,
    subsample_freq=1,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
    force_col_wise=True,
    verbosity=-1,
)


param_distributions = {
    "num_leaves": [12, 15, 20, 25, 31],
    "min_child_samples": [150, 200, 250, 300],
    "colsample_bytree": [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    "subsample": [0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
}


search_cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=3,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
)


random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=lgb_search_model,
    param_distributions=param_distributions,
    n_iter=10,
    scoring=micro_f1_scorer,
    cv=search_cv,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=1,
    verbose=1,
    refit=True,
)


random_search.fit(
    X_train_lgb,
    y_train,
    categorical_feature=LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS,
)

Parameters
estimator estimator: estimator object

An object of that type is instantiated for each grid point.
This is assumed to implement the scikit-learn estimator interface.
Either estimator needs to provide a ``score`` function,
or ``scoring`` must be passed. 		LGBMClassifie... verbosity=-1)
param_distributions param_distributions: dict or list of dicts

Dictionary with parameters names (`str`) as keys and distributions
or lists of parameters to try. Distributions must provide a ``rvs``
method for sampling (such as those from scipy.stats.distributions).
If a list is given, it is sampled uniformly.
If a list of dicts is given, first a dict is sampled uniformly, and
then a parameter is sampled using that dict as above. 		{'colsample_bytree': [0.7, 0.8, ...], 'min_child_samples': [150, 200, ...], 'num_leaves': [12, 15, ...], 'subsample': [0.8, 0.9, ...]}
scoring scoring: str, callable, list, tuple or dict, default=None

Strategy to evaluate the performance of the cross-validated model on
the test set.

If `scoring` represents a single score, one can use:

- a single string (see :ref:`scoring_string_names`);
- a callable (see :ref:`scoring_callable`) that returns a single value;
- `None`, the `estimator`'s
:ref:`default evaluation criterion <scoring_api_overview>` is used.

If `scoring` represents multiple scores, one can use:

- a list or tuple of unique strings;
- a callable returning a dictionary where the keys are the metric
names and the values are the metric scores;
- a dictionary with metric names as keys and callables as values.

See :ref:`multimetric_grid_search` for an example.

If None, the estimator's score method is used. 		make_scorer(f...average=micro)
n_jobs n_jobs: int, default=None

Number of jobs to run in parallel.
``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
for more details.

.. versionchanged:: v0.20
`n_jobs` default changed from 1 to None 		1
cv cv: int, cross-validation generator or an iterable, default=None

Determines the cross-validation splitting strategy.
Possible inputs for cv are:

- None, to use the default 5-fold cross validation,
- integer, to specify the number of folds in a `(Stratified)KFold`,
- :term:`CV splitter`,
- an iterable yielding (train, test) splits as arrays of indices.

For integer/None inputs, if the estimator is a classifier and ``y`` is
either binary or multiclass, :class:`StratifiedKFold` is used. In all
other cases, :class:`KFold` is used. These splitters are instantiated
with `shuffle=False` so the splits will be the same across calls.

Refer :ref:`User Guide <cross_validation>` for the various
cross-validation strategies that can be used here.

.. versionchanged:: 0.22
``cv`` default value if None changed from 3-fold to 5-fold. 		StratifiedKFo... shuffle=True)
verbose verbose: int, default = 0

Controls the verbosity of information printed during fitting, with higher
values yielding more detailed logging.

- 0 : no messages are printed;
- >=1 : summary of the total number of fits;
- >=2 : computation time for each fold and parameter candidate;
- >=3 : fold indices and scores;
- >=10 : parameter candidate indices and START messages before each fit. 		1

Pseudo random number generator state used for random uniform sampling
from lists of possible values instead of scipy.stats distributions.
Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple

n_iter n_iter: int, default=10

Number of parameter settings that are sampled. n_iter trades
off runtime vs quality of the solution. 		10
refit refit: bool, str, or callable, default=True

Refit an estimator using the best found parameters on the whole
dataset.

For multiple metric evaluation, this needs to be a `str` denoting the
scorer that would be used to find the best parameters for refitting
the estimator at the end.

Where there are considerations other than maximum score in
choosing a best estimator, ``refit`` can be set to a function which
returns the selected ``best_index_`` given the ``cv_results_``. In that
case, the ``best_estimator_`` and ``best_params_`` will be set
according to the returned ``best_index_`` while the ``best_score_``
attribute will not be available.

The refitted estimator is made available at the ``best_estimator_``
attribute and permits using ``predict`` directly on this
``RandomizedSearchCV`` instance.

Also for multiple metric evaluation, the attributes ``best_index_``,
``best_score_`` and ``best_params_`` will only be available if
``refit`` is set and all of them will be determined w.r.t this specific
scorer.

See ``scoring`` parameter to know more about multiple metric
evaluation.

See :ref:`this example
<sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_grid_search_refit_callable.py>`
for an example of how to use ``refit=callable`` to balance model
complexity and cross-validated score.

.. versionchanged:: 0.20
Support for callable added. 		True
pre_dispatch pre_dispatch: int, or str, default='2*n_jobs'

Controls the number of jobs that get dispatched during parallel
execution. Reducing this number can be useful to avoid an
explosion of memory consumption when more jobs get dispatched
than CPUs can process. This parameter can be:

- None, in which case all the jobs are immediately created and spawned. Use
this for lightweight and fast-running jobs, to avoid delays due to on-demand
spawning of the jobs
- An int, giving the exact number of total jobs that are spawned
- A str, giving an expression as a function of n_jobs, as in '2*n_jobs' 		'2*n_jobs'
error_score error_score: 'raise' or numeric, default=np.nan

Value to assign to the score if an error occurs in estimator fitting.
If set to 'raise', the error is raised. If a numeric value is given,
FitFailedWarning is raised. This parameter does not affect the refit
step, which will always raise the error. 		nan
return_train_score return_train_score: bool, default=False

If ``False``, the ``cv_results_`` attribute will not include training
scores.
Computing training scores is used to get insights on how different
parameter settings impact the overfitting/underfitting trade-off.
However computing the scores on the training set can be computationally
expensive and is not strictly required to select the parameters that
yield the best generalization performance.

.. versionadded:: 0.19

.. versionchanged:: 0.21
Default value was changed from ``True`` to ``False`` 		False

For instance the below given table

4.8b CatBoost Hyperparameter Tuning¶

The same RandomizedSearchCV / stratified 3-fold / Micro-F1 setup as the LightGBM search (Section 4.7), tuning CatBoost's depth, l2_leaf_reg, and learning_rate. iterations is fixed at 700 here -- the same count used for the tuned/final/CV models below -- so the search score is comparable to what those later sections actually measure. (An earlier version of this search fixed iterations=400 to save time; that let it pick a config -- depth=8, learning_rate=0.1, l2_leaf_reg=1 -- that looked best at 400 trees but overfit by 700, reporting a CV score of 0.7608 that never held up: real validation/CV performance at 700 iterations was ~0.748-0.750. Tuning and the final iteration count must match.)

In [91]:
catboost_search_model = CatBoostClassifier(
    loss_function="MultiClass",
    iterations=700,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    thread_count=-1,
    verbose=False,
)

catboost_param_distributions = {
    "depth": [4, 6, 8],
    "l2_leaf_reg": [1, 3, 5, 7],
    "learning_rate": [0.05, 0.08, 0.1],
}

catboost_search_cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=3,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
)

catboost_random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=catboost_search_model,
    param_distributions=catboost_param_distributions,
    n_iter=5,
    scoring=micro_f1_scorer,
    cv=catboost_search_cv,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=1,
    verbose=1,
    refit=True,
)

catboost_random_search.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cat_features=CAT_FEATURES,
)

print("Best parameters:")
print(catboost_random_search.best_params_)
print(f"\nBest CV Micro-F1: {catboost_random_search.best_score_:.4f}")

4.8d Ensemble (LightGBM + CatBoost) Validation Performance¶

A simple average of the two tuned models' predicted class probabilities, argmax'd back to a damage grade. Averaging two models that make somewhat different errors (LightGBM splits on native categories plus the explicit geo*_te features; CatBoost uses its own ordered target statistics) is a cheap way to pick up cases where they disagree usefully.

In [93]:
CLASS_ORDER = [1, 2, 3]

lgb_valid_proba = pd.DataFrame(
    tuned_lgbm.predict_proba(X_valid_lgb),
    columns=tuned_lgbm.classes_,
    index=X_valid.index,
)[CLASS_ORDER]

catboost_valid_proba = pd.DataFrame(
    tuned_catboost.predict_proba(X_valid),
    columns=tuned_catboost.classes_,
    index=X_valid.index,
)[CLASS_ORDER]

ensemble_valid_proba = (lgb_valid_proba.values + catboost_valid_proba.values) / 2
ensemble_valid_pred = np.array(CLASS_ORDER)[ensemble_valid_proba.argmax(axis=1)]

evaluate_model(
    "Ensemble (LightGBM + CatBoost)",
    y_valid,
    ensemble_valid_pred,
)

4.9 Stratified 3-Fold Cross-Validation¶

After selecting the LightGBM configuration, its stability is evaluated using 5-fold stratified cross-validation.

Each fold preserves the class distribution of the target. Reduced from 5 to 3 folds here (vs. the single-model version of this section) to keep runtime bounded now that two models are being cross-validated per run.

The following are reported:

  • Mean Micro-F1
  • Standard deviation
  • Minimum fold score
  • Maximum fold score
In [94]:
cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=3,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
)


lgb_cv_scores = []
catboost_cv_scores = []


for fold, (train_idx, valid_idx) in enumerate(
    cv.split(X, y),
    start=1
):
    X_fold_train = X.iloc[train_idx].copy()
    X_fold_valid = X.iloc[valid_idx].copy()

    y_fold_train = y.iloc[train_idx]
    y_fold_valid = y.iloc[valid_idx]

    fold_geo_encoder = GeoHierarchicalTargetEncoder(smoothing=(20, 40, 20))
    fold_geo_encoder.fit(X_fold_train, y_fold_train)

    X_fold_train[["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]] = fold_geo_encoder.transform(X_fold_train)
    X_fold_valid[["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]] = fold_geo_encoder.transform(X_fold_valid)

    X_fold_train_lgb, X_fold_valid_lgb = prepare_lgb_data(
        X_fold_train,
        X_fold_valid,
        LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
    )

    fold_lgb_model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
        objective="multiclass",
        num_class=3,
        n_estimators=900,
        learning_rate=0.03,
        num_leaves=random_search.best_params_["num_leaves"],
        min_child_samples=random_search.best_params_[
            "min_child_samples"
        ],
        colsample_bytree=random_search.best_params_[
            "colsample_bytree"
        ],
        subsample=random_search.best_params_["subsample"],
        subsample_freq=1,
        max_depth=-1,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        n_jobs=-1,
        force_col_wise=True,
        verbosity=-1,
    )

    fold_lgb_model.fit(
        X_fold_train_lgb,
        y_fold_train,
        categorical_feature=LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS,
    )

    lgb_fold_pred = fold_lgb_model.predict(
        X_fold_valid_lgb
    ).astype(int)

    lgb_fold_score = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        lgb_fold_pred,
        average="micro"
    )

    lgb_cv_scores.append(lgb_fold_score)

    fold_catboost_model = CatBoostClassifier(
        loss_function="MultiClass",
        iterations=700,
        depth=catboost_random_search.best_params_["depth"],
        l2_leaf_reg=catboost_random_search.best_params_["l2_leaf_reg"],
        learning_rate=catboost_random_search.best_params_["learning_rate"],
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        thread_count=-1,
        verbose=False,
    )

    fold_catboost_model.fit(
        X_fold_train,
        y_fold_train,
        cat_features=CAT_FEATURES,
    )

    catboost_fold_pred = fold_catboost_model.predict(
        X_fold_valid
    ).astype(int).ravel()

    catboost_fold_score = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        catboost_fold_pred,
        average="micro"
    )

    catboost_cv_scores.append(catboost_fold_score)

    print(f"Fold {fold}: LightGBM = {lgb_fold_score:.4f} | CatBoost = {catboost_fold_score:.4f}")

Fold 1: LightGBM = 0.7464 | CatBoost = 0.7474
Fold 2: LightGBM = 0.7505 | CatBoost = 0.7492
Fold 3: LightGBM = 0.7487 | CatBoost = 0.7478

Model Results Summary¶

All baseline/tuned models below were scored on the same held-out validation set (52,121 buildings; classes 1/2/3 with support 5,025 / 29,652 / 17,444), after adding the Section 2.1/3.2 feature engineering (structural/age features, geo frequency counts, hierarchical geo target encoding). These numbers come from a completed run made before the fix noted in Section 4.8b (CatBoost search iterations corrected from 400 to 700); re-running this notebook top-to-bottom will very likely pick a different, more regularised CatBoost configuration than the one below, since the flawed search had been favouring an under-regularised, overfitting-prone combo.

Model Micro-F1 / Accuracy Macro-F1 Weighted-F1
Logistic Regression (baseline) 0.6993 0.6745 0.7047
Random Forest (baseline) 0.7294 0.6991 0.7312
XGBoost (baseline) 0.7479 0.6987 0.7436
CatBoost (baseline) 0.7479 0.6961 0.7429
LightGBM (baseline) 0.7534 0.7082 0.7502
LightGBM (RandomizedSearchCV tuned) 0.7530 0.7079 0.7496
CatBoost (RandomizedSearchCV tuned, pre-fix params) 0.7504 0.7008 0.7457
Ensemble (LightGBM + CatBoost, tuned) 0.7541 0.7071 0.7501

Hyperparameter search (RandomizedSearchCV, 3-fold stratified CV):

  • LightGBM: best CV Micro-F1 = 0.7480, with num_leaves=25, min_child_samples=150, colsample_bytree=0.7, subsample=0.8.
  • CatBoost (pre-fix): search reported best CV Micro-F1 = 0.7608 with depth=8, learning_rate=0.1, l2_leaf_reg=1 -- but that number was measured at iterations=400 while every downstream cell fits at iterations=700. Evaluated honestly at 700 iterations, that same config only reaches ~0.748-0.750 (see the validation and 3-fold CV rows for CatBoost). Section 4.8b now searches at iterations=700 directly, so a fresh run's reported search score will be a trustworthy number instead of an inflated one -- expect it to land closer to the low-0.75s, and possibly pick a shallower/more-regularised config than depth=8.

3-fold stratified CV, tuned models (pre-fix CatBoost params, evaluated honestly at iterations=700):

  • LightGBM: Mean Micro-F1 = 0.7485, Std = 0.0021, Min = 0.7464, Max = 0.7505.
  • CatBoost: Mean Micro-F1 = 0.7481, Std = 0.0010, Min = 0.7474, Max = 0.7492.

Inference

  • Feature engineering (Section 2.1) helped the weaker baselines far more than it helped LightGBM. XGBoost jumped from a Micro-F1 in the 0.72s (raw features, ordinal-encoded geo ids) to 0.7479 once it got the engineered structural features and the geo frequency/target-encoding columns -- those columns hand XGBoost signal it can't otherwise reconstruct from ordinal-encoded high-cardinality ids. LightGBM barely moved (0.7527 -> 0.7534 baseline), because its native categorical splitting on geo_level_3_id was already extracting most of that same signal -- the new columns are largely redundant information for a model that already handles the hierarchy well.
  • CatBoost and LightGBM come out statistically tied in the 3-fold CV (0.7485 vs 0.7481, well within one fold's standard deviation), not a clear win for either -- even using the pre-fix CatBoost hyperparameters. Whatever config the corrected search finds should do at least as well.
  • Ensembling the two tuned models is the best evidenced move (0.7541 vs 0.7530/0.7504 individually). LightGBM and CatBoost make different enough errors (native category splits vs. ordered target statistics) that averaging their predicted probabilities picks up a small, real improvement. This is the version used for the final submission (Section 4.11); it is worth re-checking after a fresh run picks new CatBoost hyperparameters, since the ensemble's gain over LightGBM alone could shift.
  • Grade 1 (the minority class, 9.6% of data) remains the hardest to separate for every model -- recall sits at 0.54-0.58 across LightGBM/CatBoost/the ensemble, versus 0.84-0.85 for Grade 2. That gap, not further hyperparameter search, is where any further improvement would have to come from (e.g. per-class calibration, or accepting that the micro-F1/macro-F1 tradeoff is close to its practical ceiling for this feature set).

4.10 SHAP — Explaining the Tuned LightGBM¶

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is used to understand which features contribute most strongly to the LightGBM predictions.

This analysis focuses on Grade 3 because it represents near-total destruction.

Important:

  • SHAP magnitude measures the contribution to the model output, not a percentage probability.
  • Positive SHAP values for Grade 3 push the prediction toward Grade 3.
  • Negative values push it away from Grade 3.
  • SHAP describes model behaviour and should not be interpreted as causal evidence.
In [97]:

)

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(tuned_lgbm)

shap_values = explainer.shap_values(

)

4.11 Final Model¶

LightGBM is used as the final model because the validation and cross-validation results establish it as the strongest candidate in the pipeline.

The selected hyperparameters come from the targeted RandomizedSearchCV.

The final model is retrained using all available training observations before generating predictions for the test dataset.

In [101]:
final_geo_encoder = GeoHierarchicalTargetEncoder(smoothing=(20, 40, 20))
final_geo_encoder.fit(X, y)

X[["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]] = final_geo_encoder.transform(X)
X_test[["geo1_te", "geo2_te", "geo3_te"]] = final_geo_encoder.transform(X_test)

X_final_lgb, X_test_final_lgb = prepare_lgb_data(
    X,
    X_test,
    LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
)


final_lgbm = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    objective="multiclass",
    num_class=3,
    n_estimators=900,
    learning_rate=0.03,
    num_leaves=random_search.best_params_["num_leaves"],
    min_child_samples=random_search.best_params_[
        "min_child_samples"
    ],
    colsample_bytree=random_search.best_params_[
        "colsample_bytree"
    ],
    subsample=random_search.best_params_["subsample"],
    subsample_freq=1,
    max_depth=-1,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
    force_col_wise=True,
    verbosity=-1,
)

final_lgbm.fit(
    X_final_lgb,
    y,
    categorical_feature=LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS,
)


final_catboost = CatBoostClassifier(
    loss_function="MultiClass",
    iterations=700,
    depth=catboost_random_search.best_params_["depth"],
    l2_leaf_reg=catboost_random_search.best_params_["l2_leaf_reg"],
    learning_rate=catboost_random_search.best_params_["learning_rate"],
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    thread_count=-1,
    verbose=False,
)

final_catboost.fit(
    X,
    y,
    cat_features=CAT_FEATURES,
)

print("Final LightGBM and CatBoost fit on the full training set.")

4.12 Test Predictions¶

The final LightGBM model is used to predict the damage grade for every building in the test dataset.

In [102]:
CLASS_ORDER = [1, 2, 3]

lgb_test_proba = pd.DataFrame(
    final_lgbm.predict_proba(X_test_final_lgb),
    columns=final_lgbm.classes_,
)[CLASS_ORDER]

catboost_test_proba = pd.DataFrame(
    final_catboost.predict_proba(X_test),
    columns=final_catboost.classes_,
)[CLASS_ORDER]

ensemble_test_proba = (lgb_test_proba.values + catboost_test_proba.values) / 2

test_predictions = np.array(CLASS_ORDER)[ensemble_test_proba.argmax(axis=1)]

print("Number of test predictions:", len(test_predictions))
print("\nPrediction distribution:")
print(
    pd.Series(test_predictions)
    .value_counts(normalize=True)
    .sort_index()
    .mul(100)
    .round(3)
)

4.13 Submission File¶

The submission contains:

  • building_id
  • damage_grade

The original test-set building ID order is preserved.
